text: Miyazaki described the Night in an IGN interview as a kind of natural disaster, a cataclysm that occurred without design or intent.
The theorist suggests the Night is a natural force that was suppressed by the Golden Order for a long time, similar to how Rot was once an accepted force before being sealed away and vilified.
The Night is associated with darkness, which the ever-burning light of the Erdtree has long kept at bay.
The Night is associated with fate as read in the stars, a fate obscured by the Golden Order's bright light.
The Night represents equanimity, coming to all beings equally, contrasting with the Golden Order's selective bestowal of grace.
The theorist believes the Night Lord is a calamity caused by the suppression of grace, a natural reckoning that was long overdue.

The theorist speculates that the Trace of Night depicts the silhouette of a cosmic Outer God of Night, and proposes that white light manifesting from the tree could literally be this Outer God appearing in the world.
The Nightfarers are shown opposing this white light during the expedition's climax, suggesting hostility toward this cosmic manifestation.
The theorist believes the Recluse's Remembrance bone-like stone belongs to the Outer God of Night specifically, since the Night can also snuff out grace and is weak to holy damage.
The theorist speculates the Rune of the Coming Night may have been removed from the Elden Ring, always been separate from it, or broken away during the Shattering.
The imagery of the Night Lord crawling from a pile of bodies evokes the Divine Gate or the Jar Saints' conglomerations of bodies used to touch the divine via the Crucible.
The theorist compares the Night Lord harboring the Primordial Night Lord's Rune within himself to how Marika harbors the Elden Ring.
The theorist believes the man who took in Gladius on a rainswept night was Heolstor, the Nameless Night Lord.
Every Night Lord carries a piece of Heolstor's Night, making them all in some sense aspects of the original Night Lord.
The theorist believes the people buried in the Round Table crypt belonged to, or inherited the burden of, the Cutting-Gifted Tribe.

The theorist draws a parallel between the Cutting-Gifted Tribe and the base game's prophets who foresaw the burning of the Erdtree and were persecuted and forced to wear shackles as a warning, with both remaining loyal to the Erdtree despite their punishment.
The theorist suggests the cross-legged commoner figure seen at the end of the game belongs to the Cutting-Gifted Tribe, based on his common garb.

A horticultural cutting is a piece of a parent plant used to grow a genetically identical clone, distinct from grafting, which combines two different plants; the theorist concludes the Cutting-Gifted Tribe were given a cutting of a tree so significant it became central to their tribal identity.

The theorist believes the Cord End is the frayed end of a sacrificed girl's hand bindings, left behind as a quiet act of rebellion to lead others to the secret location, and suggests the sacrificial twigs implicate the Erdtree in the ritual sacrifice of young girls, since Cord Ends are found exclusively in Erdtree churches.

The theorist speculates that the 'cuttings' gifted to the tribe may have been people rather than plant matter, specifically the young sacrificed girls, described as 'cuttings of Marika,' comparing this to known examples of people merged with great trees such as Miquella and the Haligtree, or Miranda of the Flower Crucible.
The theorist proposes that the sacrificed girl surrounded by dried branches became or created the divine dried white spirit tree that defies the Night, found in Nightreign's Round Table Hold area.

The theorist compares this scheme to Marika's past behavior, noting it would be like her to prepare contingencies against the Night, condemning the ancients just as she condemned the Tarnished, only to recall them when needed to her Round Table Hold.
The theorist theorizes that the 'branches' sent to distant lands were actually the progeny of the Cutting-Gifted Tribe, who became the bloodline of the Nightfarers scattered across many peoples.

The theorist considers that the 'formless master' could be an Outer God given the term's resemblance to other formless entities like Bloodborne's Formless Oedon and Elden Ring's Formless Mother, but ultimately suggests it is more likely the grace within the Hold, interpreted by the Duchess as Marika.

Just as Marika binds Hugh (Hoarah Loux) to the Roundtable Hold until he forges a god-slaying weapon in the base game, the Nightfarers are similarly bound to their Hold until the Night Lord is defeated, at which point the Hold ceases to exist.

The theorist frames the Erdtree's unexplained original sin as a recurring FromSoftware plot device, paralleling how Gwyn suppressed the dark and Marika suppressed death, suggesting the suppression of the Night is the Erdtree's original sin.
What unites all Night Farers is not power, destiny, or virtue, but a shared experience of loss, failure, or incompleteness that mirrors Limveld's own unfinished, interrupted nature.

The Revenant's uncertainty about their own continuity mirrors Limveld's own unresolved relationship to the Lands Between, both being defined by an ambiguous answer to whether resemblance equals sameness.
The first night represents the least activated state of the cosmological cycle that the three nights embody.
By the end of the second night, Limveld has mostly transformed into what it currently is, rather than remaining a memory of what it used to be.
The darkness of the third night is described as the presence of something other than light, which is the native medium of the Night Lords and makes them most powerful there.
Although Limveld resets physically between expeditions, the Night Lords are implied to carry forward awareness of previous expeditions and challenges by Nightfarers.
Each expedition is framed as part of an ongoing repeated practice rather than a one-time test, with prior expeditions contributing to future attempts.
Gladius embodies the Golden Order's principle of martial excellence with the aspect of service, devotion, and justice stripped away, leaving only the excellence itself as an end.
Maris is connected to the lands between's mythology of outer gods and the association of water with memory and ancient, persistent forces.
Equilibrian's catastrophe is one of perfect stalemate rather than defeat, reflecting a world that has lost the capacity to resolve its internal tensions.
Together, the six Night Lords (Gladius, Libra, Maris, Equilibrian, Balancer, Dreglord) form a complete taxonomy of forces unleashed by Limveld's catastrophe.
The Forsaken Hollows' hostility is interpreted as an expression of sudden, severe loss and pain rather than deliberate malice.
Defeating Balancer is interpreted as a symbolic payment toward the debt rather than its cancellation.
Dreglord's existence implies that Limveld's civilization and the broader cosmic processes shaping the Lands Between generated discarded 'dregs' on a massive scale over a long time.
It is ambiguous whether the Finger Readers in Limveld are interpreting nothing out of habit or are receiving guidance from some other source occupying the Two Fingers' role.
Every ending in Nightreign answers the same underlying question from different angles: given full understanding of what Limveld is, what do you do about it.
The stability ending is incomplete because the cosmic forces represented by the Night Lords are not destroyed, only suppressed into the background of Limveld, requiring ongoing maintenance to last.
The remain-in-Limveld endings share a common theme of accepting impermanence as a condition of existence rather than a problem to solve.
This success-where-civilization-failed ending is framed as the most thematically hopeful conclusion, demonstrating that what was lost in the catastrophe is not permanently beyond recovery.
Limveld is characterized as a world that fundamentally asks to be understood rather than merely survived or conquered.
Nightfarers who achieve the deepest endings succeed because of their attentiveness to the world rather than their combat skill alone.
Nightreign's central thematic question is how to respond to a repeating cycle that one can see clearly but may not be able to escape, framed through the three-night expedition cycle.
The eight Nightfarers collectively represent a complete set of human responses to loss.
Wylder represents the response of letting go of a lost thing entirely and finding sufficiency in what remains.
Duchess represents the response of carrying loss as identity, making the loss the foundation of a continued sense of self.
Guardian represents the response of treating loss as obligation, using past failure as the basis for renewed commitment.
Recluse represents the response of treating loss as information, studying what was lost to understand what the losing revealed.
Ironeye represents the response of acceptance, incorporating loss into a way of being shaped by but not defined by absence.
Raider represents the response of continuation, carrying a lost thing forward in practice even after it no longer exists.
Executor represents the response of interrogation, questioning what the lost thing actually was and whether it deserved the commitment it received.
Revenant represents the response of uncertainty, being unable to determine whether the self that continues after loss is the same self that existed before it.
Nightfarers resting at uncertain sites of grace are depicted as trusting an unreliable connection in order to receive necessary renewal, a metaphor for faith.

After each expedition's third night ends, surviving Nightfarers earn a 'morning' that is described as real but provisional, since the Night Lords' forces remain present in the world's cosmological background.
Nightfarers who learn to distinguish the sounds of the old world from the transformed world are considered to have the deepest, most embodied understanding of Limveld.
According to a servant of the Round Table, each Nightfarer committed a grave misdeed, which is why they were chosen as 'seekers of redemption.'
The Cutting-Gifted Tribe does not appear directly in the game, but its name may relate to 'grafting,' connecting it to themes of combining or splicing in Elden Ring lore.
The Elden Ring games reference an 'original sin,' with Miquella's Great Rune and Mohg's remembrance both alluding to a hidden original sin, possibly tied to Marika's ascension to godhood.
The ritual implied by Cord's End resembles the fate of Marika's shaman people, who were melded into saints by the Hornsent in Shadow of the Erdtree.

The theory is that the Cutting-Gifted Tribe tried and failed to create their own Erdtree-like structure to stop the Night, then became the spiritual foundation of the Round Table to guide future descendants (the Nightfarers) to succeed where they failed.
The Duchess faces a dilemma: defeating the Night Lord will kill her (tied to the Round Table) while keeping the Night going would save Wilder from his injury-caused death.
The Guardian ultimately finds a new sense of purpose and belonging among the Nightfarers, considering them his new flock after losing his original one.
Those who come into contact with death-related corruption become 'those who live in death,' considered heretical undead by the Golden Order.
The concept of animism, the belief that objects and creatures possess spiritual essence, may underlie the Revenant's origin as a doll gaining a soul.

It is implied that the infant created by the Recluse eventually became the Night Lord, though its growth afterward may have been driven by its own choices; the legend of the Knight who died to a hero may represent this transformation.

The Night Lord may be an amalgamation of multiple beings, suggested by its three arms, unusual design seen in one of the game's endings, and his wielding of the Dark Moon Greatsword among other weapons.
The Executor's journal entries appear to be written from both his and the painter's perspectives, creating ambiguity between a guest, an executioner, and a painter.
One theory holds that the Executor killed the first Crucible Knight but failed to protect the painter, or chose to kill her himself rather than let another executioner do so.
It is unclear whether the Executor or the painter was truly from the Land of Reeds, since Chapter 2's line about being 'an artist from the distant land of Reeds' may belong to the painter instead.
The Executor's fragmented memory and his fight against the Executor's Cry are tied to unresolved guilt over the painter's death and the Erdtree's destruction.
The Executor appears to seek redemption by defeating the Night Lord responsible for destroying the Erdtree's light, symbolically completing his unfinished painting of the tree.
Noster's full title is 'Wisdom of Night,' and its name may derive from Greek roots related to knowledge, matching this title.
Maris's name likely derives from the Latin 'Stella Maris,' meaning star of the sea, and its title 'Fathom of Night' references measuring ocean depth.

Several Night Lord enemies, such as Libra, Fulgor, Maris, Gladius, and Noster, appear thematically connected to astrology and constellations: Libra directly references the zodiac sign of the scale symbolizing balance; Fulgor's centaur design may reference Sagittarius though it wields a sword rather than a bow; Maris's cosmic appearance may parallel the Elden Beast's design; and Canis Major and Scorpius may tie to Gladius (the Dog Star) and Noster (linked to a bug nebula in Scorpius), respectively.
Adel and Caligo, both dragons, lack clear ties to star signs or constellations unlike the other Night Lords.
The Night seems to both harm and help these creatures, starving Adel and displacing Noster while giving purpose to Libra and Maris.

Heolstor shares color palette and elemental traits with the other Night Lords, suggesting he encompasses aspects of them all, and may be the physical embodiment of the concept of Night, paralleling how the Elden Beast embodies the Greater Will's concept of Order, functioning as a vessel for the darkness of Night rather than its true source.
The Nox now live underground awaiting a new Lord of Night, which may be connected to Nightreign's Night Lord.

This suggests the Nightfarers survive their ordeal and are returned to their respective worlds once their quests are complete, possibly representing a resetting of the timeline so that the Night's conquest of the Lands Between never truly happened.
This giant's face resembles the Night Lord's helmet, suggesting it may be the Night Lord or another aspect of the Night, implying the Erdtree's presence had suppressed its total destruction.
The Formless Mother may be connected to the Two Fingers, Miquella, or the Greater Will, any of whom could be the true force communicating through the Duchess.

Marika may be the 'cheated god' referenced in Nightreign's lore, tying the original sin from Elden Ring to the first sin referenced in Nightreign, which would imply she punished a tribe for uncovering a hidden truth, though this concept may be entirely unique to Nightreign without basis in Elden Ring.
This implies Margit continues to protect the Erdtree and Elden Throne even in Nightreign's altered timeline, despite being an Omen.
This suggests Godrick grafted a Crucible Knight or being with Crucible traits onto himself at some point, though the victim's identity is unknown.
Nightreign's Nokstella could be the same Eternal City referenced in Elden Ring's lore.
